children: For many analysts and investors, the Tesla-SpaceX merger is a fait accompli. There is just one problem. SpaceX stock isn't keeping up its part of the bargain.
Merger speculation has raged for months, ratcheting even higher after CEO (of both companies) Elon Musk told investors that both boards had formed committees to look at a deal on Oct. 20.

The logic of a combination is relatively simple. Create a vertically integrated AI leader that controls everything from power generation to chip manufacturing to AI models, as well as virtual and physical AI applications, including AI agents and humanoid robots.

Conventional Wall Street wisdom sees SpaceX as the acquirer, paying a premium for Tesla in an all-stock deal. But the better Tesla stock does, and the worse SpaceX stock does, the more expensive the deal gets for SpaceX shareholders.

SpaceX shares are down about 12% since its blowout third-quarter numbers on Oct. 21, falling as fears about AI finance and growth rise. Tesla stock is flat over the same span, despite reporting its own so-so third-quarter results.

At a 15% premium for Tesla shareholders, SpaceX would be giving Tesla investors about 3.2 shares. Tesla investors would end up owning more than 50% of the company, based on the fully diluted share count, according to FactSet.
The question is: Will SpaceX shareholders accept that? If the answer is no, then the question becomes: Will Tesla shareholders accept a smaller premium?
Things looked easier when SpaceX stock was $200. At that point, a 15% premium would have been only 2.3 SpaceX shares. SpaceX shareholders would have ended up owning about 57% of the combined company.

Who owns more might not matter. Elon Musk tends to get what he wants. But the more shares SpaceX issues, the higher the risk of a Marvell-Lumentum-type reaction. Both stocks were weak in early November after Marvell agreed to acquire Lumentum in an all-stock deal. Earlier in the year, with Marvell stock closer to its 52-week high of $330, it would have had to issue far fewer shares to create similar economics for Lumentum shareholders.
Merger math can be funny from time to time. The answer to the problem isn't difficult: SpaceX shares need to start performing soon — or there might be no merger math to do.
SpaceX stock was up 0.1% in premarket trading Thursday at $139.88, while S&P 500 futures were down 0.4% and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 0.1%. Tesla stock was down 0.5% at $388.70.
